landmarks.name: Anibare Bay
landmarks.writeup: A scenic bay known for its white sandy beaches and clear waters, popular for swimming and snorkeling.

wiki.extract: Anibare Bay is a large bay located in the Anibare district of eastern Nauru, a small island nation located in Oceania.

landmarks.name: Command Ridge
landmarks.writeup: The highest point on Nauru, offering panoramic views of the island and remnants of World War II fortifications.

wiki.extract: Command Ridge is considered the highest point of Nauru, with an elevation of 65 metres (213 ft).

landmarks.name: Moqua Well
landmarks.writeup: An underground freshwater lake that serves as a natural water source and a cultural site.

wiki.extract: The Moqua Well is a small underground lake in Yaren, Nauru.

cultural_events.name: Angam Day
cultural_events.writeup: A national holiday celebrating the survival and resilience of the Nauruan people.

cultural_events.name: Nauru Independence Day
cultural_events.writeup: Commemorates Nauru's independence from Australia, New Zealand, and the United Kingdom on January 31, 1968.

wiki.extract: The Nauru Independence Act 1967 is an act of the Parliament of Australia which resulted in the independence of Nauru and the end of its status as a UN trust territory administered by Australia.

food_writeup: Nauruan cuisine features seafood, coconut, and tropical fruits, with traditional dishes often incorporating fish, pandanus, and breadfruit.
brief_history: Nauru was first inhabited by Micronesian and Polynesian people. It became a German colony in the late 19th century, later administered by Australia, New Zealand, and the UK. It gained independence in 1968. The island's economy was historically based on phosphate mining.

important_people.name: Hammer DeRoburt
important_people.description: First President of Nauru and key figure in independence.

current_conflicts: Nauru faces environmental challenges due to phosphate mining and economic dependency issues but has no active armed conflicts.

commentary.inflation_management: Nauru uses the Australian dollar, so inflation is imported - and the early-2000s phosphate-economy distortions made it extreme: 19.3% in 2006 and a series high of 22.4% in 2009, followed by deflation of -3.4% in 2011 as the economy restructured. The 2010s were calmer (mostly 0-10%), but inflation picked up again to 9.3% in 2024 with a projected 6.1% for 2025. There is no domestic monetary policy; price stability depends on Australian conditions and on the government's ability to smooth costs using processing-centre and mining revenues.
commentary.debt_management: Nauru's debt history is the Pacific's most extreme: the IMF series (which starts in 2009; 2006-08 are missing) shows gross debt at 295.6% of GDP in 2009 and a series high of 298.9% in 2010 - the legacy of phosphate-era borrowing against a depleted resource. What followed was a two-decade workout: debt fell to 113% by 2015, 56.3% in 2020, and a projected 14.6% in 2025, driven by GDP growth ($0.03bn to $0.18bn), Australian processing-centre payments, and restructurings. The overhang is essentially cleared, but the episode is a cautionary tale about resource-curse borrowing. Note the 2006-08 data gap in the IMF series.

key_events.event: The IMF series carries no debt data for these years, reflecting the opacity of the phosphate-era debt overhang at its worst.
Australia reopened the offshore Regional Processing Centre, making asylum processing Nauru's main revenue source.
October: David Adeang became president, shifting the country's political direction.
January: severed ties with Taiwan and recognized Beijing, two days after Taiwan's presidential election.

commentary.outlook_next_decade: The debt workout is essentially complete, which is a genuine achievement, but Nauru's economy still rests on two fragile pillars: Australian processing-centre payments (subject to Canberra's politics) and phosphate remnants. Diversification options are minimal on a 21-square-kilometre island. The China switch may bring infrastructure finance. The base case is fiscal stability with high revenue volatility; the risk is a sudden loss of the processing-centre income that underwrites the budget.
commentary.caveat: Outlook is an analytical assessment as of October 2026, not a forecast. 2025 figures are IMF estimates/projections.
